summary: Describes models for deploying DNSSEC when an enterprise uses several DNS providers for its authoritative service. Difficulties can arise depending on features in use, especially when each provider signs the zone with its own keys. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary:
DNSSEC signs a domain's records so that a resolver can prove they were not altered. This RFC looks at the case where a company uses two or more DNS providers at once and each one signs the records.

The fix is to share the signing keys between the providers. The company then has to coordinate every key change across all of them.

questions: how to use dnssec with multiple dns providers
what is a combined signing key
how do key rollovers work with multiple dns providers
what is a multi-signer dnssec model
how do dnssec key rollovers work with several providers
subtitle: How to run DNSSEC when two or more DNS providers each sign the same zone with their own keys.

tldr.problem: An enterprise often uses several DNS providers for its authoritative service. When each provider signs the zone with its own keys, a validating resolver can receive a signature it is unable to check against the keys it has already cached.
tldr.mechanism: Two models are described. In both, every provider's DNSKEY RRset carries the zone signing keys of all providers. In Model 1 the zone owner holds one common Key Signing Key; in Model 2 each provider has its own and the parent zone holds a DS record for each.
tldr.outcome: Resolvers need no changes, but the zone owner must coordinate every key rollover across the providers and keep the key-management APIs strongly authenticated.

Signing algorithm
facts.value: One common algorithm, or a common set

facts.label: Rollover methods assumed
facts.value: Double-Signature for KSK, Pre-Publish for ZSK

today: RFC 8901 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes two workable ways to run DNSSEC across several signing providers and leaves the details of a provider-to-provider key exchange protocol to a future document should there be interest in one.

sections.title: Why Several Providers Complicate DNSSEC
sections.content:
Many enterprises hire more than one Domain Name System (DNS) provider to run their authoritative DNS service. The reason is redundancy: the service then survives a complete failure of any single provider. There are other reasons too. An enterprise or a provider may need a DNS feature that standard zone transfer cannot carry, or a provider may insist on re-signing the records itself with its own keys.

When standard zone transfer works, none of this changes the normal deployment. One entity signs the zone, which may be the zone owner, one of the providers or a third party, and the providers act as secondary authoritative servers.

When zone transfer cannot be used, the picture changes. Each provider becomes a primary server in its own right, signing the data it receives from the zone owner and serving it to resolvers. That configuration, where several parties sign the same zone, is what this RFC is about.

The RFC assumes the reader knows DNS operations and points to "DNS Terminology" in RFC 8499 for the terms it uses.
sections.plainLanguage:
Companies often buy DNS service from more than one supplier so that a failure at one does not take their domain offline. But each supplier signs the domain's records with its own keys.

That is where the difficulty starts.

sections.title: Two Ways to Share One Zone
sections.content:
In both models, every provider publishes the same set of zone signing keys, so that a resolver has a path to authenticate whatever it is served. The zone owner normally updates each provider through that provider's own interface, and relies on the provider to do the signing. The models do not require the providers to talk to each other, because managed-DNS providers tend to have a contractual relationship only with the zone owner. If the parties are willing, a protocol for direct key exchange could be written later.

These models also work for the nonstandard DNS features mentioned earlier, as long as the provider can sign the answers it generates. Because those answers are often produced at query time, the provider may sign them on the fly, or it may precompute every possible answer with its signature and pick the right one when the query arrives.

In Model 1, the zone owner holds the Key Signing Key (KSK), manages the DS record set in the parent zone, and signs the apex DNSKEY RRset before handing it to the providers. Each provider has its own Zone Signing Key (ZSK) set for signing zone data. The zone owner's interface lets it query the providers for their public ZSKs and insert one combined DNSKEY RRset holding every provider's ZSKs and the KSK, signed by the KSK. Even when the contents do not change, the zone owner must re-sign that RRset periodically as the signature approaches expiry, and redistribute it.

In Model 2, each provider holds its own KSK and its own ZSKs. Each provider's interface lets the zone owner import the other providers' ZSKs into its DNSKEY RRset. Each provider then signs the DNSKEY RRset with its own KSK, and the zone owner keeps a DS RRset in the parent zone holding one DS record per provider, each pointing at a different KSK.

Model 1 cannot be combined with a Combined Signing Key, where one key does the work of both the KSK and the ZSK, because the zone owner would then hold the only signing key and the providers could not sign their own data. Model 2 has no such problem: any or all providers may use a combined key, the parent DS record then points at that key, and the public key has to be imported into the other providers' DNSKEY RRsets.
sections.plainLanguage:
In both models, every provider publishes the signing keys of all the other providers. That way a resolver can check a signature no matter which provider answered.

The difference is who holds the top-level key. In Model 1 the zone owner holds one key that everyone trusts. In Model 2 each provider has its own, and the parent zone holds a record for each of them.

sections.title: What Happens When a Resolver Cannot Check a Key
sections.content:
The central requirement for both models is that the zone signing keys of all providers are present in each provider's DNSKEY RRset, and that the set is vouched for by the single KSK in Model 1 or by each provider's KSK in Model 2. If that is not done, a resolver can get stuck. With two providers, A and B, the failure looks like this:

  • The resolver follows a secure delegation to the zone.
  • It fetches the DNSKEY RRset from a name server belonging to Provider A, authenticates it against the parent DS RRset, and caches it.
  • Later it resolves a name in the zone while that cached RRset is still usable, and this time it queries a name server belonging to Provider B.
  • The answer is signed by Provider B's ZSK, which the resolver cannot authenticate, because that ZSK is not in the cached DNSKEY RRset.

The resolver will not accept the answer. It may still get an authenticated result by trying other name servers until one of Provider A's answers, but it pays for extra round trips, with the latency and processing that come with them, and the number of extra trips depends on the resolver's name server selection and on how many servers Provider B runs. It may also simply fail, either because it gave up after a number of retries or a delay, or because the client waiting for the answer timed out.

How the DNSKEY RRset itself is authenticated differs between the models. In Model 1, one KSK managed by the zone owner signs an identical RRset deployed at each provider, and the signed DS record in the parent points at that KSK. In Model 2, each provider has a distinct KSK and signs the RRset with it, and the parent holds several DS records. Either way, the resolver can authenticate whichever provider's RRset it receives.

The providers must also use a common signing algorithm, or a common set of algorithms. The specifications require that when a DNSKEY RRset holds several algorithms, the records in the zone are signed with at least one key of each algorithm. If the providers chose different algorithms, that requirement cannot be met.
sections.plainLanguage:
A resolver caches the keys it learned from one provider. If it later asks a different provider and gets an answer signed with a key it has never seen, it cannot check that answer and has to try again.

The fix is simple to state: make sure every provider publishes every provider's keys.

sections.title: Authenticated Denial Across Providers
sections.content:
Authenticated denial lets a resolver prove that a name does not exist. An authoritative server returns signed NSEC records, or the hashed NSEC3 records of RFC 5155, that carry the proof. NSEC3 adds the option to opt out of signing insecure delegations and gives some protection against walking a zone to enumerate its names.

These responses are self-contained, so the resolver needs no extra queries to complete the proof. That is why switching a signed zone between NSEC and NSEC3 needs no key rollover.

It also means different providers can use different methods for the same zone. Doing so, though, throws away the zone-enumeration defence of NSEC3, because an attacker can simply enumerate the zone by asking the providers that use NSEC. A better configuration has every provider use a method that keeps the defence, such as precomputed NSEC3, NSEC3 white lies, or NSEC black lies. Providers offering different methods may, however, make it harder for resolvers to cache negative answers well.

The usual arrangement is that one method is used everywhere, because the behaviour is well defined and closest to normal practice. Resolvers are expected to cope when different servers for the same zone answer with different methods, since that is already seen while NSEC and NSEC3 are being switched or when NSEC3PARAM is updated. Some resolver software handles a single transition between two configurations better than it handles a permanent mixture, which can make caching less efficient and can push more queries to the authoritative servers. That matters in particular with "Aggressive Use of DNSSEC-Validated Cache", RFC 8198. If the providers cannot all use the same method, the RFC recommends keeping the number of distinct configurations as low as possible, and notes that providers all using NSEC3 with different NSEC3PARAM values already count as a mixed setup.
sections.plainLanguage:
DNSSEC can also prove that a name does not exist. Two methods do this, and one of them makes it harder for an attacker to list every name in the zone.

If providers disagree on the method, the protection weakens. The RFC asks for as little disagreement as possible.

sections.title: Rolling Keys and Moving Them Between Providers
sections.content:
Rolling a key means replacing it. The RFC assumes the Double-Signature method for Key Signing Keys and the Pre-Publish method for Zone Signing Keys, both described in RFC 6781, and that there are two providers. Other methods can be adapted with small changes. Timing follows the recommendations in that RFC, but with the extra steps these models add: the time to propagate data to all authoritative servers now also includes the time to import the new keys into each provider.

In Model 1, a KSK rollover starts with the zone owner generating a new KSK and collecting the DNSKEY RRset from each provider. The new key goes into each provider's RRset, the RRset is signed with both the old and the new key, and it is sent back to each provider. The zone owner then points the parent DS RRset at the new key and, once the DS record time to live has expired, removes the old key from the RRset. A ZSK rollover is similar but starts at the provider: the provider generates a new ZSK and asks the zone owner to insert it into every provider's DNSKEY RRset, because the zone owner signs that RRset. The zone owner then waits until all zone data has been re-signed by the new key and has propagated, plus the longest zone time to live of anything signed by the old key, before the old key is removed.

In Model 2, a KSK rollover by Provider A does not touch Provider B's DNSKEY RRset, but the parent DS RRset must be updated, so the zone owner is still involved. A ZSK rollover by Provider A starts with A adding the new key to its own RRset and re-signing it with its KSK. The zone owner then imports that key into the other providers' RRsets, and A waits for the DNSKEY time to live, the import time and the propagation time before it starts signing zone data with the new key.

The CDS and CDNSKEY records, which automate the exchange of secure entry point keys between parent and child, work in these models too. In Model 1 the changes are centralised at the zone owner, which still has to push the updated signed records down to the providers. In Model 2 the key-management mechanism has to support cross-importation so that every provider has a common view of the record set that the parent can see.

The RFC does not design a new interface. It lists the functions a provider's existing interface must offer: a way to read the current DNSKEY RRset; for Model 1, a way to import a signed DNSKEY RRset and replace the current one; for Model 2, a way to import a DNSKEY record from another provider. DNS UPDATE and the Extensible Provisioning Protocol can partly stand in for these. Once the providers have bootstrapped each other's keys this way, they could also query each other's DNSKEY RRsets, check the signatures, and import or withdraw keys automatically as rollovers happen.

One practical consequence is that the DNSKEY RRset grows, so the answer to a DNSKEY query grows with it. With newer elliptic-curve algorithms the keys are small enough that the answer stays well below the usual path maximum transmission unit, so fragmentation, truncation and TCP fallback are unlikely to matter. Operators still need to be able to emit and handle large DNS responses over UDP, and a move to DNS over TLS or DNS over HTTPS may make the question moot.
sections.plainLanguage:
Keys have to be replaced from time to time, and with several providers every replacement touches all of them. The RFC walks through the steps for both models, for both kinds of key.

It also lists what a provider's programming interface has to be able to do, since the providers are not expected to talk to each other directly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
These models necessarily put private signing keys in the hands of third-party providers. The zone owner is choosing to place a great deal of trust in them. The more traditional arrangement, where the zone owner runs a hidden master and uses zone transfer, is arguably more secure, because only the zone owner holds the signing keys and a provider cannot serve false data without a validating resolver detecting it.

The interfaces used to import and export keys must be strongly authenticated, so that a malicious party cannot tamper with key material. Providers commonly offer REST interfaces over HTTPS with client authentication such as a username and password or an API key, and the HTTPS layer gives transport security and server authentication. Multifactor authentication can strengthen this further. If DNS mechanisms such as UPDATE are used to insert or delete keys, they need strong authentication too, for example with Transaction Signatures (TSIG) as in RFC 2845. Key generation and other security operations should follow the guidance in RFC 6781.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing keys now sit with outside providers, so the zone owner is trusting them. The interface that moves keys around must be strongly protected, or someone could tamper with the keys.
